stops.name: Carthage rising, Qart-Hadasht, the New City
stops.campa: Walls climb the Byrsa in courses of dressed stone; the double harbor is cut from the shore, one basin for trade and one, hidden, for warships not yet built; streets are laid out, laws given, and the city takes the name the Tyrians give any daughter-town: Qart-Hadasht, the New City, which the Greeks and Romans will shorten to Carthage. Word of the queen who measured a kingdom out of an ox-hide runs down the African coast and across the sea to Tyre itself, and settlers of every neighboring people begin to ask leave to build within her walls.

stops.name: Carthage, the temple of Tanit and the queen's court
stops.campa: On the height above the harbor Elissa raises the first temple of the goddess the Tyrians know as Astarte and the Carthaginians will come to call Tanit, Face of Baal, whose sign, the sharp triangle beneath a crossbar and a disc, will one day stand on ten thousand stelae across this country. Around her she gathers a senate drawn from the Tyrian exiles and the Libyan and Cypriot families who have joined the founding, and rules as queen and priestess both, a widow who answers, the sources agree, to no man's authority but her own vow to Sychaeus.

stops.name: Carthage, the tribute treaty and the city's fame
stops.campa: The Libyans, having granted the ground, now claim a yearly rent for it, and Elissa's Carthage pays what is owed, a due the city will render for generations until its own strength outgrows the need. Trade multiplies: purple, silver, grain, the old Tyrian routes now doubled from a second hearth on the African shore. Ambassadors come from the towns nearby to treat with the widow-queen as an equal power, and the histories mark this as the moment Carthage stops being an exile's camp and becomes, in fact as in the omen of the horse's head, a nation.
stops.quote: An annual tribute being fixed for the ground which it was to occupy.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)

stops.name: Carthage, suitors from every neighboring throne
stops.campa: The queen's fame as a builder of cities draws suitors from every neighboring court, each wanting the new power on the coast bound to his own house by marriage; each, the sources agree, she refuses, holding to her single vow that no man will have what she gave once to Sychaeus and will not give twice. Her own councilors grow uneasy at the refusals, fearing the anger of kings so near and so strong. Among the suitors turned away is Iarbas, king of the Gaetulian tribes of the interior, who will not accept a widow's no as any kingdom's last word.

stops.name: The storm off the Libyan coast, a fleet driven onto her shore
stops.campa: The poets fold time as they please, and in their telling, Virgil's above all, Carthage stands already risen when Juno, who hates the Trojan race and dreads the empire fated to grow from it, buys the wind-king Aeolus and hurls a storm on seven ships fleeing burning Troy. Battered hulls limp toward Libya on a sea Elissa's own sailors once crossed as exiles themselves. Whether the years truly meet or the poem alone bends them together, the tradition holds this second landing as sacredly as the first, and both are hers to receive.
stops.quote: Quos ego—! Sed motos praestat componere fluctus.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.135 (Neptune's unfinished threat, calming the storm that wrecks the Trojans on her coast)

stops.name: The shore, Venus tells Aeneas of the widowed queen
stops.campa: Aeneas, walking the woods above the cove where his storm-scattered men have landed, meets a huntress who is his own mother Venus in disguise. She tells him whose city climbs the hill before him: Dido, she calls her by the byword now attached to her name, a Tyrian widow who fled her brother's blade and built a New City here by her own wit, still faithful to a dead husband, still ruling alone. Then the goddess wraps her son and Achates in cloud, unseen, and sends them up toward the walls Elissa raised with an ox-hide's worth of cunning.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.340-341 (Venus naming Dido, 'fleeing her own brother')

stops.name: Juno's temple, the queen enthroned before the murals of Troy
stops.campa: Elissa comes to the half-built temple of Juno in the morning brightness of her own city, radiant among a hundred attendants, to give judgment and assign the year's labors like a second Diana among her nymphs. Aeneas, still hidden in the cloud, watches her take her seat on a high throne and sees, painted on the temple's walls, the whole war of Troy: Priam, Achilles, Hector dragged in the dust; pity for a grief the world already knows, rendered in color before he has said a single word of it himself.
stops.quote: Sunt hic etiam sua praemia laudi; / sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.461-462 (Aeneas before the murals, of the queen's own temple)

stops.name: The banquet, 'what dreams alarm my anxious mind'
stops.campa: That evening Elissa receives the storm-lost Trojans at her own table, generous as she has been to every exile since her own exile began, and asks the stranger who steps from the cloud like a god to tell the whole tale of Troy's fall from the beginning. Venus has sent Cupid in the shape of little Ascanius to sit warm in the queen's lap; unknowing, she drinks in a love that will unmake the vow she has kept seven years to Sychaeus's memory. Before the night is over she confesses to her sister Anna a terror she cannot yet name.
stops.quote: Anna soror, quae me suspensam insomnia terrent!
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.9 (Dido to her sister Anna, the morning after)

stops.name: The cave, the hunt, the storm, and the marriage she names herself
stops.campa: Juno and Venus, each for her own ends, contrive it: on a royal hunt a black storm breaks over the ridges, and Elissa and the Trojan leader take shelter in the same cave while the company scatters. Lightning stands for their wedding-torch, the mountain nymphs cry out on the heights, and from this day she no longer hides the love or names it fault, but calls it marriage: the first cause, the poets will always say, of all her sorrow and her death, though she believes, that one afternoon, that she has kept faith rather than broken it.
stops.quote: Coniugium vocat, hoc praetexit nomine culpam.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.172 (of Dido after the cave)

stops.name: The confrontation, 'did you hope, false one, to hide so great a crime?'
stops.campa: Rumor, swift and monstrous, has run the winter long through the Libyan towns while the two forget their kingdoms; now Elissa sees the Trojan ships being quietly fitted for sea and confronts him where he directs the work in a Tyrian cloak she gave him. She calls him faithless, asks whether her hospitality, her hand, her whole ruined name in the mouths of the neighboring kings, count for nothing beside a fate he claims but she cannot see. He answers only that Italy calls him against his own will; she does not believe a god can command a man to break a woman so completely.
stops.quote: Dissimulare etiam sperasti, perfide, tantum / posse nefas tacitusque mea decedere terra?

stops.name: The last letter, her own testament, before the fire
stops.campa: In the poets' fullest reckoning of her own voice, Elissa writes a last letter to the departing Trojan, reproaching him one final time and dictating, in the same page, the words she wishes cut on her own tomb: that he gave her both the cause of her death and the blade, and that her own hand alone struck the blow. It is the epitaph of a woman who will not let even her murderer's memory soften what was done to her, nor let her own choice at the end be taken from her and laid at any door but her own.
stops.quote: Praebuit Aeneas et causam mortis et ensem; / ipsa sua Dido concidit usa manu.
stops.quote_source: Ovid, Heroides 7.195-196 (Dido's self-composed epitaph, in her letter to Aeneas)

stops.name: The pyre, her last words, and the curse of the avenger unborn
stops.campa: At dawn she sees the harbor empty and the sails gone. She has built a great pyre, telling her household it is a rite to unbind her love, and now climbs it holding the sword he left behind; from its height she curses him and all his line: let a nameless avenger rise out of her own bones to hunt his settlers with fire and iron, shore against shore, forever, then speaks her true last words, and falls upon the blade. Far out at sea Aeneas looks back and sees the walls of Carthage lit with her fire.
stops.quote: Vixi et quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi, / et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.653-654 (Dido's last words: 'I have lived, and finished the course that fortune gave')
